abstract: As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream. Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always fulfill requests successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.

sections.body: Existing benchmarks study experience reuse and adaptation, but task success alone cannot show whether agents update outdated experience while keeping parts that remain valid. The authors introduce ReScopeBench, which spans 18 interactive environments. It separates **structural experience** (how resources are organized and accessed) from **rule experience** (reusable principles and constraints). Tasks reuse discoverable experience, and local changes are unannounced, so agents must detect them through interaction. Discovery and execution run under resource budgets. The benchmark scores task results together with saved experience. Across 20 commercial and compact open-weight models, retaining experience improves average task performance. Agents generally record structural experience more completely than rule experience.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing benchmarks rarely show which experience agents revise, retain, or lose when environments change silently.

sections.body: Each environment is a simulated application with reproducible initial states and tools whose outputs reflect the current state. Discoverable experience is identified from environment code and data, verified through tool interactions, and linked into a private dependency graph. Ordered task streams of 16, 24, or 32 tasks share resource relationships and operating rules, and changes are scheduled before selected tasks. Changes are detectable through tool observations but are not announced. Verification replays reference solutions and checks outputs, budgets, and grader scores. The benchmark has 352 tasks across 18 environments and nine application domains, with 3–18 tools per environment (10.1 on average) and 26 changes. Scores for BP, EP, DP, SC, RC, UC, and RT each range from 0 to 100.
sections.heading: ReScopeBench
sections.headline: ReScopeBench builds task streams around shared experience and inserts silent environmental changes that invalidate parts of it.

sections.body: The authors run 20 models on 18 environments, with paired streams that include or clear retained experience. Deterministic graders score tasks, and GPT-6 Astra scores saved experience against reference rubrics. Gains accumulate across tasks, but change onsets interrupt them. In the 24-task group, structural coverage falls by 18.92 points at T09, and rule coverage falls by 15.97 points at T17. The compact Qwen3.8-27B records 29.05% of required updates after the first affected task, close to the commercial median of 29.75%. Structural coverage exceeds rule coverage for 17 of 20 models, with a mean gap of 4.79 points. Over the first four affected tasks, replacement-content coverage rises from 21.47% to 64.63%, while still-valid coverage stays between 88.07% and 91.07%. Coverage spans the full reference inventory, so it does not directly measure delivery of a specific request.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Experience-enabled scores reach 81.12 at best, but no model exceeds 37.63 in update coverage after change.

sections.body: Experience-based adaptation methods differ in what they keep from interaction. Reflexion and ExpeL turn feedback and trajectories into reflections or reusable insights. Voyager stores executable skills, and Agent Workflow Memory abstracts recurring action sequences into reusable workflows. Dynamic Cheatsheet revises test-time memory as new evidence arrives. Memory benchmarks such as LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and MemBench test reasoning over supplied histories, and MemoryAgentBench adds incremental learning and selective forgetting. Interactive and skill-oriented benchmarks study reuse, while AgingBench and EvoArena examine maintenance as information and conditions change. ReScopeBench assesses saved content alongside task outcomes, separating correction of affected relationships from retention of those that remain valid.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work adapts agent experience through reflections, skills, and workflows, while ReScopeBench adds evaluation of how it is maintained under change.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the benchmark. Experience-first construction builds tasks around shared structural and rule experience, then adds silent changes that invalidate selected content. Across 20 models, retaining experience improves task performance. Rule experience is generally recorded less completely than structural experience. Agents preserve much still-valid content but leave required updates incomplete. They can also fail to complete requests even when the required experience is correctly recorded. More interaction after change does not always coincide with more attempts to update saved experience. The authors position ReScopeBench as a testbed for agents that selectively revise outdated experience and apply what they retain effectively.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Agents keep much still-valid experience but leave updates incomplete and can fail requests despite correct records.

sections.body:
The appendix covers the following:
- **Environments and changes:** Table 3 lists task goals, stream lengths, and tool counts for 18 environments. Table 4 lists all 26 scheduled changes with their mechanisms.
- **Evaluation details:** Temperature 1 and top-p 0.95 where set, 100 agent iterations per task, up to 65,536 output tokens per response, memory limited to 16,000 characters, skills limited to 100,000 characters, and history tools capped at 30 calls per task.
- **Judge consistency:** GPT-6.1 Sol rejudged all 7,040 checkpoints, agreeing on 98.79% of structural and 99.24% of rule claim decisions.
- **Supplementary analyses and cases:** Tool use, request-level action paths, and two illustrative cases, including a Oracle Clinical One task with a 17-unit budget.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the 18 environments and 26 scheduled changes, evaluation and judging details, extra analyses, and case studies.
